title: Satyavati
hook: Satyavati finally tells Bhishma about the boat, the island and her firstborn, and calls Vyasa with a thought
carry: she thinks of him; he comes

segments.voice: Yesterday, Satyavati asked Bhishma to break his vow, and he would not give up truth — "I will not give up truth." Who is your promise still for? Today ends the week. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

Bhishma has refused her, but he doesn't leave her empty-handed. He reminds her of old stories, of lines that were carried on in hard times when a learned man was invited to father children for a house that had none. Find such a man, he says. And Satyavati, the text says, smiles, and her voice falters with shyness. Then the queen mother tells the stepson something she has carried since before she ever saw a palace.
screen: `FIND A LEARNED MAN.` → `SHE SMILES, AND FALTERS.` → `A SECRET FROM THE RIVER.`

segments.voice: She tells him about the boat. About the sage Parashara, the mist on the Yamuna, the son born on an island. She tells him that son is Dvaipayana, the great sage people call Vyasa, and that when he left, he promised to come whenever she thought of him. If you agree, she says, I'll think of him now. Bhishma agrees. And Satyavati thinks of her son. That's all it takes. Vyasa appears, the text says, at once. He bows to his mother, and she weeps and holds him, and tells him plainly what the house needs. Now look back over the week. It began with a father's boon sealing Bhishma's vow, the vow that let a fisherman's daughter's sons rule. Then we went back to her beginning: a baby found in a fish, a boat, the fragrance she asked for, a son's promise. Then the losses came one by one: a husband, a proud son killed by his namesake, a young king dead of sickness. Three princesses were brought from Kashi, and Amba spoke and was let go. Then the queen asked Bhishma to take back his vow, and he wouldn't. And now, at the end, the one door left open is the one she opened herself, years ago, in a boat on a river. A woman who started as a ferry girl has become the person holding the house of the Kurus together. Some readers see in her a schemer; some see a survivor; the text gives her its last word today: she remembers, and her son comes.
screen: `THE BOAT, TOLD AT LAST.` · `SHE THINKS OF HIM. HE COMES.` · `A WEEK OF LOSSES.` · `FROM FERRY GIRL TO QUEEN MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath move without help. Satyavati called her son with a single thought. So, gently, think of someone. Not to ask them for anything. Just let a face come, someone who once said they'd be there. Notice what happens in your body when they arrive in your mind: the chest, the throat, the hands. Let them stay a while. If you pray, you might hold them there in your own words. Then come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Satyavati. The fisherman's daughter who became queen mother of the Kurus, and kept one door open to her firstborn.
Your line: she thinks of him; he comes. Today, think of someone who once promised to come when you needed them, and send them a word. Day seven hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: In Hindu tradition Vyasa is honored as the sage who arranged the Vedas and composed the Mahabharata, and in this part of the poem he steps into the story he tells.

pairs: comes when she thinks of him

myth: he told old stories and said to find a learned man.
Vyasa came the moment Satyavati thought of him
just as he'd promised when he left the island.
Satyavati told her secret to no one
she told Bhishma, smiling and shy, and he agreed.

fork.setup: you're Satyavati. Bhishma says to find a learned man for the house. you have a son no one knows about. what do you do?
options: keep the secret and let Bhishma search.
fork.reveal: she tells him about the boat and the island, and with his agreement thinks of Vyasa, who comes at once.

original.note: Sanskrit Vyasa: the name the sage Dvaipayana is known by, Satyavati's firstborn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a queen with a hidden past.
what it means: the son whose promise she kept is the one who saves her house.
what a scholar hears: Vyasa, the poem's own credited author, now walks into the story he tells.
